title: Commensurate with the Needs - Canadian SR&ED Glossary
description: Understand the phrase Commensurate with the Needs in our Canadian SR&ED glossary and how it governs eligible R&D support work claims.
summary: Under paragraph 248(1)(d) of Canada's Income Tax Act, support work claimed by SR&ED taxpayers—engineering, design, computer programming, data collection, testing or psychological research—qualifies only when it is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research or experimental development carried out in Canada; performed as standalone commercial work, it is ineligible.

1. Executive Legislative Overview and Statutory Architecture
1.1 Dual-Mechanism Structure of the Federal SR&ED Regime

The Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program represents the cornerstone of federal industrial innovation policy in Canada, operating as the single largest federal program supporting business research and development. Administered jointly by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), which oversees operational compliance, technical review, and financial verification, and the Department of Finance Canada, which formulates legislative tax policy, the program delivered $4.6 billion in investment tax credits across 23,677 processed claims during the 2025–2026 fiscal cycle. Unlike discretionary grant mechanisms that depend on competitive budget allocations and ministerial approvals, the SR&ED regime is a statutory entitlement codified within the Income Tax Act (ITA), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) and the Income Tax Regulations (ITR), C.R.C., c. 945, guaranteeing tax relief to any taxpayer—whether a corporation, unincorporated individual, trust, or partnership—that substantiates qualifying scientific or technological investigation carried out in Canada.

The federal statutory architecture delivers a dual fiscal benefit through two distinct but interconnected statutory mechanisms that operate in tandem to reduce both taxable income and net tax payable. First, under subsection 37(1) of the ITA, a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may pool all qualifying current SR&ED expenditures—and, for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, qualifying capital SR&ED expenditures—incurred in the taxation year. This subsection 37(1) expenditure pool provides a 100% deduction against business income for tax purposes in the year the expenditures are incurred, or the taxpayer may elect to defer all or any portion of the pool deduction indefinitely to offset taxable income in future taxation years. This indefinite carryforward mechanism is particularly critical for pre-revenue biotechnology, clean technology, and deep-technology enterprises whose ordinary non-capital loss carryforwards would otherwise remain subject to fixed statutory expiration horizons.

Second, in addition to the full income deduction under section 37, the taxpayer earns an SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) calculated under subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the ITA at either the enhanced rate of 35% or the basic rate of 15% of the taxpayer's "qualified expenditures". Pursuant to section 127.1 of the ITA, this credit is either fully or partially refundable as a direct cash payment to qualifying corporations and individuals with no tax payable, or non-refundable and available to offset federal Part I tax payable with a three-year carryback and 20-year carryforward horizon.

To prevent duplicative tax relief between the section 37 income deduction and the section 127 investment tax credit, paragraph 12(1)(v) and paragraph 37(1)(e) of the ITA enforce a mandatory pool reduction and income inclusion mechanism. Specifically, the exact dollar amount of any federal SR&ED ITC claimed in a taxation year—whether applied to offset federal Part I tax payable or received as a cash refund under section 127.1—reduces the taxpayer's subsection 37(1) deductible SR&ED expenditure pool in the immediately following taxation year. If the federal ITC claimed in the prior year exceeds the remaining balance in the subsection 37(1) pool in that subsequent year, the resulting negative pool balance is brought directly into the taxpayer's taxable income under paragraph 12(1)(v) of the ITA. In parallel, provincial and territorial R&D tax credits constitute "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) and subsection 127(18) of the ITA, thereby reducing both the subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool and the federal qualified expenditure base in the taxation year in which the provincial or territorial credit is earned.
1.2 The 2024–2026 Federal Legislative Modernization Package

Between April 2024 and March 2026, the federal SR&ED regime underwent its most consequential statutory expansion since the modern framework was established in 1985, reversing capital expenditure restrictions that had been enacted in the 2012 Federal Budget and substantially broadening access to refundable credits for scaling domestic innovators. The legislative evolution unfolded across a sequence of policy consultations, fiscal updates, and statutory enactments that reshaped the economics of industrial research in Canada.

In early 2024, the Department of Finance Canada initiated formal public consultations on modernizing the SR&ED program alongside parallel consultations evaluating the creation of a Canadian patent box regime designed to encourage the domestic development and retention of intellectual property. Both Phase 1 consultation processes closed on April 15, 2024. When the federal government tabled Budget 2024: Fairness for Every Generation on April 16, 2024, the Minister of Finance announced a second phase of SR&ED consultations focused on technical eligibility reforms and extending the enhanced 35% credit rate to Canadian public companies. Budget 2024 backed this modernization mandate with an initial fiscal commitment of $600 million over four years commencing in 2025–2026, with $150 million per year committed on an ongoing basis. As complementary innovation measures, Budget 2024 introduced an immediate 100% accelerated Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) write-off for costs related to patents, data network infrastructure equipment, computers, and other data-processing equipment acquired on or after April 16, 2024, and before January 1, 2027, while allocating $14.5 million over two years to Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada's (ISED) Innovation Asset Collective to assist small and medium-sized enterprises with intellectual property creation and retention, alongside $2.4 billion to bolster Canadian artificial intelligence compute infrastructure and adoption.

Following the conclusion of the Phase 2 technical consultations, the federal government unveiled comprehensive structural reforms in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES) on December 16, 2024, which were subsequently translated into detailed draft legislative proposals released by the Department of Finance on August 15, 2025. Effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (that is, after December 15, 2024), the 2024 FES initially proposed raising the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC from $3.0 million to $4.5 million, expanding the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from the historical $10 million–$50 million range to a widened $15 million–$75 million corridor, extending eligibility for the 35% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), introducing an elective gross revenue phase-out structure for Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs), and restoring the eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs for property acquired after December 15, 2024.

Before the interim $4.5 million expenditure limit was enacted into law, the federal government tabled its November 4, 2025 Federal Budget, which further increased the annual SR&ED expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC from $4.5 million to $6.0 million, effective retroactively for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. Implemented through Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, this legislative package doubled the maximum annual federal refundable cash credit available to qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs from the historical $1.05 million ceiling to $2.1 million ($6,000,000 multiplied by 35%) on qualifying current expenditures.

body.text: 2. Scientific and Technological Eligibility: Statutory Definition and Administrative Framework
2.1 Subsection 248(1) Categories of Eligible Work and Statutory Exclusions

To qualify for federal and provincial SR&ED tax incentives, claimed activities must strictly satisfy the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" set out in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. The opening words (the chapeau) of the statutory definition mandate that the work constitute a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". Once this threshold methodological requirement is satisfied, the work must fall within one of four exhaustive categories of eligible activity enumerated in paragraphs (a) through (d) while avoiding the seven statutory exclusions listed in paragraphs (e) through (k).

The first two eligible categories encompass pure and directed scientific research: basic research under paragraph 248(1)(a), defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view, and applied research under paragraph 248(1)(b), defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Basic research typically occurs in foundational physics, chemistry, molecular biology, or theoretical computer science where the researcher seeks to uncover underlying natural laws or phenomena without targeting an immediate commercial product, whereas applied research pursues new scientific knowledge directed toward a defined industrial or medical utility.

The third and largest category is experimental development under paragraph 248(1)(c), which is defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Experimental development accounts for the vast majority of corporate SR&ED claims in Canada. Crucially, the statutory wording establishes a rigorous legal distinction between the technological advancement (which requires advancing the underlying technological knowledge base or capability) and the commercial objective (creating or improving the material, device, product, or process); even incremental improvements to existing industrial processes or software systems qualify under paragraph (c) provided that achieving those improvements requires resolving a genuine technological uncertainty through systematic experimentation or analysis.

The fourth eligible category is support work under paragraph 248(1)(d), which encompasses work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. This statutory provision is vital in practice: routine computer programming, computer-aided design (CAD), mathematical modelling, or physical testing is completely ineligible when performed as a standalone commercial engineering activity, but becomes 100% eligible under paragraph 248(1)(d) when it is directly required to construct, execute, and validate an experiment designed to resolve a scientific or technological uncertainty under paragraphs (a), (b), or (c). Notably, paragraph (d) explicitly includes psychological research as an eligible support work category when it is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of eligible scientific research or experimental development—such as human-factors cognitive load experimentation in aerospace cockpits or medical device interfaces—even though research in the social sciences and humanities is otherwise excluded from standalone eligibility.

Even where an enterprise conducts sophisticated technical work within the broader lifecycle of an R&D project, paragraphs (e) through (k) of subsection 248(1) explicitly exclude seven categories of activity from constituting SR&ED. Paragraph (e) excludes market research or sales promotion, which bars consumer preference surveys, market validation beta-testing, and competitive product benchmarking. Paragraph (f) excludes quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes, thereby eliminating standard quality assurance (QA/QC) compliance runs, routine regulatory or UL/CSA certification testing where no technological obstacle arises, and standard software regression testing. Paragraph (g) excludes research in the social sciences or the humanities—including economics, business management, sociology, law, and linguistics—except to the narrow extent that psychological research qualifies as direct support work under paragraph (d). Paragraph (h) excludes prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas, meaning that geological field exploration is barred even though developing a novel metallurgical extraction process or an experimental downhole telemetry tool qualifies as experimental development under paragraph (c). Paragraph (i) excludes the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process, establishing a strict statutory boundary once technological uncertainty is resolved and commercial manufacturing commences. Finally, paragraph (j) excludes style changes—cosmetic, aesthetic, or ergonomic alterations that do not entail overcoming underlying structural or functional technological constraints—and paragraph (k) excludes routine data collection, where standard operational, environmental, or financial logs are gathered outside a specific experimental hypothesis.
2.2 The CRA 2021 Eligibility Guidelines: The "Why" and "How" Framework

On August 13, 2021, the Canada Revenue Agency archived its former Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (which had governed claims since 2012 and 2015) and replaced it with the consolidated Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives. While the underlying statutory text of subsection 248(1) remained unchanged, the CRA reorganized its administrative review methodology around two overarching foundational questions—Why the work was conducted and How the work was conducted—which are applied by CRA Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) through a sequential three-question administrative test.

The first administrative pillar—the "Why" requirement—asks why the work is being conducted: it must be undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement. In operational terms, a technological advancement can only be pursued if the taxpayer confronts a scientific or technological uncertainty—a system-level limitation, physical constraint, or resource conflict in the underlying science or technology whose resolution cannot be determined or predicted in advance on the basis of generally available scientific or technological knowledge or standard engineering practice. The CRA enforces a sharp distinction between technological uncertainty and business, financial, or project uncertainty. Not knowing whether a product can be built within budget, whether customers will adopt a feature, or how a poorly documented third-party software library operates does not constitute a technological uncertainty. Rather, technological uncertainty arises only when competent professionals in the relevant field cannot predict whether a proposed architecture, material formulation, or physical process can overcome competing technical constraints—such as processing 10 million concurrent event streams with sub-100-millisecond latency on memory-constrained commodity hardware.

The second administrative pillar—the "How" requirement—asks how the work is being conducted: it must be carried out by means of a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology through experiment or analysis. Under the 2021 CRA Guidelines, demonstrating a systematic investigation requires establishing four sequential operational elements. First, the researcher must define the scientific or technological obstacle or uncertainty by documenting the baseline of existing knowledge and explaining why standard engineering procedures are inadequate. Second, the researcher must generate a specific hypothesis—defined as an idea consistent with known scientific or technological facts that serves as a starting point for further investigation toward achieving an objective or resolving the problem, expressed as a proposed causal mechanism, design, or mathematical model. Third, the researcher must test that idea or hypothesis by means of planned experiment or analysis, recognizing that the hypothesis will naturally evolve and iterate as testing reveals unexpected failure modes. Fourth, the researcher must develop logical conclusions based on the quantitative and qualitative results or findings of the experiment or analysis, while maintaining contemporaneous evidence generated as the work progresses.

A foundational principle of Canadian SR&ED law is that commercial or technical success is not required for work to qualify. When a taxpayer conducts a rigorous, systematic investigation to test a hypothesis and the experimental findings conclusively falsify that hypothesis—proving, for example, that a novel composite polymer fractures under thermal cycling or that a distributed consensus algorithm deadlocks under network partitioning—the elimination of that unviable technological pathway advances the general state of technological knowledge and fully qualifies for the SR&ED tax credit. Conversely, ad hoc trial-and-error troubleshooting—randomly adjusting configuration parameters or swapping hardware components until a device functions without formulating and testing a causal hypothesis explaining why the failure occurs—fails the "How" requirement and is systematically disallowed on audit.
2.3 Sector-Specific Eligibility Nuances: Software Engineering, Artificial Intelligence, and Advanced Manufacturing

Because software development, artificial intelligence (AI), and advanced manufacturing account for the largest volume of Canadian SR&ED claims—and simultaneously attract intense audit scrutiny from CRA technical reviewers—delineating the boundary between routine commercial engineering and eligible experimental development is essential.

body.text: In manufacturing, metallurgy, chemical processing, and hardware design environments, a recurring audit focal point involves experimental production (shop-floor SR&ED) versus commercial production. While paragraph 248(1)(i) strictly excludes commercial production, CRA administrative policies and Tax Court of Canada jurisprudence recognize that experimental development of an industrial manufacturing process frequently cannot be validated at a laboratory bench scale and must instead be tested on full-scale commercial production lines due to scale-dependent fluid dynamics, heat transfer, or mechanical tolerances. During such experimental production runs, the incremental labour, consumed raw materials, and dedicated equipment usage directly required to execute the experimental trial and measure process variables qualify as SR&ED expenditures, provided the primary purpose of the run is resolving technological uncertainty rather than fulfilling commercial customer orders, and subject to statutory ITC recapture if any marketable trial output is subsequently sold.
3. Judicial Precedents and Tax Court of Canada Jurisprudence
3.1 The Foundational Five-Question Test in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants

While the CRA's 2021 administrative guidelines organize eligibility around the "Why" and "How" pillars, the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal have repeatedly held that CRA administrative policies are merely interpretive guidelines, do not carry the force of law, and cannot narrow or supersede the statutory text of subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. In Canadian tax jurisprudence, the authoritative legal interpretation of subsection 248(1) remains the landmark decision of Justice Donald Bowman (later Chief Justice of the Tax Court of Canada) in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen , [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 D.T.C. 1839 (T.C.C.).

In Northwest Hydraulic, the taxpayer conducted physical scale-model hydraulic engineering investigations of river systems, dams, and spillways across five representative engineering projects. Rejecting the Crown's position that physical scale modelling using established fluid mechanics principles constituted mere "routine engineering," Justice Bowman articulated the canonical five-question judicial test for determining whether a particular technical venture constitutes SR&ED. As confirmed in subsequent Tax Court decisions such as Lehigh Hanson Materials Limited v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 205 (at para. 37) and Clevor Technologies Inc. v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 166 (at para. 11), a taxpayer appealing an SR&ED disallowance must answer each of the five Northwest Hydraulic questions in the affirmative on a balance of probabilities.

The first question asks: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? Justice Bowman defined the term "routine engineering" as referring to "techniques, procedures and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field" (at para. 16). Where the resolution of a technical problem cannot be reasonably predicted using established practice and publicly available scientific or engineering knowledge, genuine technological uncertainty is established.

The second question asks: Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty? Justice Bowman specified (at para. 16) that satisfying this second criterion entails a structured five-stage sub-process: (i) the observation of the subject matter of the problem; (ii) the formulation of a clear objective; (iii) the identification and articulation of the technological uncertainty; (iv) the formulation of a hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty; and (v) the methodical and systematic testing of the hypothesis. Crucially, Justice Bowman emphasized that while initial uncertainties are identified at the outset of a project, an integral hallmark of genuine SR&ED is the emergence and identification of new technological uncertainties as the research progresses, requiring the researcher to apply the scientific method to uncover, recognize, and resolve those cascading uncertainties.

The third question asks: Did the procedures adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of the hypotheses? The procedures must be characterized by trained and systematic observation, quantitative measurement, and experiment. At the same time, Justice Bowman explicitly recognized that "intuitive creativity and even genius may play a crucial role in the process for the purposes of the definition of SRED," provided that such intuition and creativity operate within the total discipline of the scientific method rather than unstructured guesswork.

The fourth question asks: Did the process result in a technological advancement, that is to say an advancement in the general understanding? By "general understanding," Justice Bowman clarified that the knowledge sought must advance what is known to, or available to, competent persons knowledgeable in the field—not merely fill a subjective knowledge gap of an inexperienced employee learning standard industry techniques. Provided the overall approach is aimed at achieving a scientific or technological advancement over the public baseline, incremental advancements and conclusive rejections of unviable hypotheses fully satisfy this fourth requirement.

The fifth question asks: Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results kept as the work progressed? Although the statutory text of subsection 248(1) does not explicitly contain the word "contemporaneous," Justice Bowman held that maintaining a detailed record of hypotheses, experiments, and test results as the work progresses is an inherent attribute of the scientific method and a vital evidentiary requirement under subsection 230(1) of the ITA.
3.2 Appellate Affirmation and Evidentiary Standards: RIS-Christie, C.W. Agencies, and National R&D

Following the Tax Court's ruling in Northwest Hydraulic, the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) elevated Justice Bowman's five-question framework into binding national precedent while clarifying the evidentiary standards required to substantiate testing in court. In RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen , [1999] 1 C.T.C. 132, 99 D.T.C. 5087 (F.C.A.), the Federal Court of Appeal endorsed Justice Bowman's analytical framework and focused specifically on the fifth criterion concerning documentary evidence of systematic testing. Writing for the appellate panel, Justice Robertson held that scientific research inherently requires repeatability and verifiability. For an experimental test to be repeatable and verifiable by technical peers or the judiciary, the claimant must produce objective, contemporaneous documentary records demonstrating what tests were conducted, when they took place, and what quantitative or qualitative results were obtained; retrospective oral testimony presented years later at trial is legally insufficient to discharge the taxpayer's burden of proof when documentary records of test results are missing.

Shortly thereafter, in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen , 2001 FCA 393, the Federal Court of Appeal distilled and formally adopted the five Northwest Hydraulic questions as the definitive appellate test governing all SR&ED eligibility disputes in Canada. More recently, in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada , 2021 FCA 88, and National R&D Inc. v. Canada , 2022 FCA 72, the Federal Court of Appeal reaffirmed that the binding legal interpretation of subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act remains the five-question common-law test established in Northwest Hydraulic; the CRA's August 2021 restructuring of its administrative eligibility guidelines around the "Why" and "How" questions does not alter that test. In National R&D, the appellate court confirmed both that a claimant cannot bypass the requirement of systematic experimentation and contemporaneous evidence merely by asserting a novel software concept, and that CRA administrative policy updates cannot alter the statutory criteria affirmed by the appellate courts.
3.3 Specialized Jurisprudence on Contractual Control, Commercialization Boundaries, and Multidisciplinary R&D

Beyond the foundational five-question test, specialized decisions of the Tax Court of Canada govern recurring structural disputes involving contractual SR&ED ownership, post-commercialization engineering, and non-traditional industries.

Under paragraph 37(1)(a) and paragraph 248(1)(d) of the ITA, expenditures qualify only where the SR&ED is undertaken "by or on behalf of" the taxpayer. When Corporation A contracts Corporation B to design or develop a custom technical system, contentious audit disputes frequently arise when both the customer and the contractor attempt to claim SR&ED tax credits on the same underlying technical work, or when the CRA disallows the contractor's claim on the ground that the work was performed "on behalf of" the commissioning client. In Hypercube Inc. v. The Queen , 2015 TCC 65, and Concept Danat Inc. v. The Queen , 2019 TCC 32, the Tax Court of Canada examined the underlying commercial contracts, intellectual property ownership clauses, assumption of financial and technological risk (contrasting fixed-price deliverable contracts where the vendor bears the risk of technological failure against time-and-materials R&D service mandates), and the degree of technical specification and control exercised by the customer to determine which entity legally conducted the SR&ED on its own behalf.

The boundary between ongoing experimental development and commercial release was addressed in 6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen , 2015 TCC 77. In that case, the appellant engineered an ultra-compact mobile printer that integrated multiple contributing engineering disciplines into a miniature form factor where no publicly available technical literature provided design guidance. While the CRA's National Technology Sector Specialist allowed the SR&ED claims for the 2006 and 2007 taxation years—recognizing that multidisciplinary integration into an unprecedentedly small footprint constituted a genuine technological advancement—the CRA disallowed the appellant's 2009 and 2010 claims primarily because the printer had been released to commercial manufacturing in the interim. The Tax Court scrutinized this administrative cut-off, establishing that while commercial manufacturing itself is excluded under paragraph 248(1)(i), the mere fact that an initial product version has been commercially released does not automatically disqualify subsequent systematic R&D if fundamental technological challenges and specification failures remain unresolved.

In Life Choice Ltd. v. The Queen , 2017 TCC 21, the Tax Court evaluated nutraceutical and biochemical formulation projects—specifically investigating how to neutralize the cyano-toxicity of amygdalin for safe daily human consumption and how to replicate the metabolic effects of acetyl-L-carnitine and alpha-lipoic acid. The Court rejected the suggestion that references by Justice Bowman and the Federal Court of Appeal to "technological" uncertainty restricted the five-question test to experimental development, holding that the Northwest Hydraulic framework applies with equal statutory force to scientific research (basic and applied) and experimental development. Furthermore, in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King , 2024 TCC 159, the Tax Court overturned the Minister's disallowance of a 2020 SR&ED claim involving food science and thermal canning processes. The Court observed that while facing an uncertain commercial path toward an objective is not by itself sufficient to qualify as SR&ED, Manning Canning successfully demonstrated on a balance of probabilities that it confronted non-routine technological uncertainty, formulated targeted hypotheses, executed a disciplined scientific method, sought an advancement in general technological understanding, and maintained contemporaneous records as the work progressed.
4. Federal Investment Tax Credit Rates, Expenditure Limits, and Refundability Mechanics
4.1 Enhanced (35%) Versus Basic (15%) Federal Investment Tax Credit Tiers

The federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit operates on a two-tier flat rate structure—an enhanced rate of 35% and a basic rate of 15%—governed by the legal classification of the corporate or individual claimant, the nature of the expenditure (current versus capital), and the corporation's annual expenditure limit.

Following the enactment of the 2024–2026 legislative reforms (effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024), access to the 35% enhanced refundable tier is no longer restricted exclusively to Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs). In a historic structural shift, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)—defined as public corporations resident in Canada whose shares are listed on a designated stock exchange, that are not controlled directly or indirectly in any manner whatever by one or more non-resident persons, and that satisfy consolidated gross revenue thresholds—may now claim the 35% enhanced refundable ITC on up to $6.0 million of qualified SR&ED expenditures annually.

body.text: 4.2 Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Mechanics: Taxable Capital Versus Gross Revenue Election

Under subsection 127(10.1) and subsection 127(10.2) of the ITA, the maximum annual expenditure limit eligible for the 35% enhanced rate is $6,000,000 for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, doubled from the $3,000,000 ceiling that applied to prior taxation years. Where a corporation is associated with one or more other corporations in a taxation year (within the meaning of section 256 of the ITA), the $6,000,000 expenditure limit must be shared and allocated among the associated corporate group.

Historically, a severe structural limitation of the SR&ED program was that capital-intensive start-up and scale-up enterprises—such as clean technology, semiconductor, robotics, aerospace, and clinical-stage life sciences companies—raised institutional venture capital or debt financing to construct laboratories and pilot plants, which inflated their "taxable capital employed in Canada" (calculated under Part I.3 of the ITA) above $10 million long before the enterprise achieved commercial profitability, prematurely phasing them out of the 35% refundable credit. To eliminate this penalty on capital formation, the 2024–2026 legislative reforms enacted two complementary phase-out regimes for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024.

Under the first regime—the Expanded Taxable Capital Phase-Out ($15 Million to $75 Million)—the lower taxable capital threshold at which the expenditure limit begins to decrease was raised from $10 million to $15 million, and the upper ceiling at which the expenditure limit is completely eliminated was raised from $50 million to $75 million of taxable capital employed in Canada by the corporation and its associated corporate group in the immediately preceding taxation year. Expressed mathematically, for a CCPC (and its associated group) with prior-year taxable capital (TC) (where $15 million < TC < $75 million), the annual Expenditure Limit (EL) is determined by the linear formula: EL = $6,000,000 × ($75,000,000 − TC) ÷ $60,000,000.

Consequently, for every $10 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada in excess of $15 million, the $6.0 million expenditure limit is reduced by $1, reaching zero when prior-year taxable capital reaches $75 million. By comparison, for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the $3.0 million expenditure limit phased out linearly between $10 million and $50 million of prior-year taxable capital.

Under the second regime—the Alternative Gross Revenue Phase-Out Structure (Mandatory for ECPCs, Elective for CCPCs)—the $6.0 million expenditure limit is phased out on a straight-line basis by reference to the corporation's (and its consolidated or associated corporate group's) average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years. While Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) must determine their expenditure limit using this average gross revenue metric, a CCPC is now legally entitled to elect to have its expenditure limit determined under the gross revenue phase-out formula instead of the taxable capital formula. This election provides transformative flexibility for venture-backed CCPCs that carry more than $15 million—or even more than $75 million—in balance-sheet equity and debt capital to fund multi-year hardware or clinical R&D while generating minimal pre-commercial revenue, allowing them to preserve the full $6.0 million expenditure limit and $2.1 million annual cash refund.
4.3 Carryback, Carryforward, Pool Deduction, and ITC Recapture Rules

When an SR&ED Investment Tax Credit is non-refundable—such as the 15% basic credit earned by a foreign-controlled corporation, a large public corporation, or a CCPC/ECPC on expenditures exceeding its $6.0 million expenditure limit (where the 40% refundability test is not met), or the 60% non-refundable portion of capital ITCs—the credit is governed by the carryback and carryforward rules under subsection 127(5) and subsection 127(9) of the ITA. Unused non-refundable SR&ED ITCs may be carried back up to three preceding taxation years to offset federal Part I tax paid in those prior years (generating a cash refund of previously remitted corporate income taxes), or carried forward for up to 20 subsequent taxation years to offset future federal Part I tax payable. Should a corporation undergo a de jure acquisition of control (a change of control), its unused subsection 37(1) SR&ED expenditure pool and unused SR&ED ITC carryforwards become subject to the statutory loss-streaming rules under subsection 37(6.1) and subsections 127(9.1) and (9.2) of the ITA, meaning they may only be deducted or claimed in post-acquisition taxation years if the corporation continues to carry on the business in which the SR&ED occurred for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, and only against income from that same or a similar business.

Conversely, whenever a taxpayer claims an SR&ED ITC on the cost of materials transformed into a prototype or commercial batch, or on restored capital property acquired after December 15, 2024, and within 20 years of acquisition the taxpayer sells the property or converts it to commercial use, the statutory ITC recapture provisions in subsections 127(27) through 127(35) of the ITA are triggered. Under subsection 127(27), the taxpayer must add directly to its federal Part I tax payable for the year of disposition or conversion an amount equal to the historical ITC percentage (15% or 35%) multiplied by the lesser of the original qualified expenditure cost of the property and the proceeds of disposition (or the fair market value of the property at the time it is converted to commercial use). To maintain tax integration, any recaptured ITC amount is simultaneously added back to the taxpayer's subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool (or affects capital cost allowance and unclaimed capital expenditures) in the year of recapture so that the taxpayer recovers ordinary tax depreciation or cost-of-sales deductibility.
5. Qualifying Expenditures, Overhead Elections, and Quantitative Stacking Mechanics
5.1 Directly Engaged Salaries and Wages: Non-Specified Versus Specified Employees

Salaries and wages incurred in respect of employees who are directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada constitute the primary expenditure base for the vast majority of Canadian claimants. Only the proportion of an employee's working time spent directly performing basic research, applied research, experimental development (paragraphs 248(1)(a)–(c)), or commensurate support work (paragraph 248(1)(d)), including direct first-line technical supervision of hands-on SR&ED personnel, qualifies for inclusion. Time spent on general corporate administration, human resources, legal affairs, accounting, sales, or high-level executive oversight not directly tied to technical experimentation is excluded from directly engaged salaries and is instead accounted for through the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount or tracked under the Traditional Method. Furthermore, under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) of the ITA, salaries and wages paid to Canadian-resident employees performing permissible SR&ED outside Canada (where the foreign work is directly undertaken by the taxpayer as an integral part of a Canadian SR&ED project and cannot be conducted in Canada due to specialized geographical, environmental, or facility constraints) may be included up to a strict statutory ceiling of 10% of the total salaries and wages directly attributable to SR&ED carried on in Canada.

The Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations enforce a strict statutory bifurcation between Non-Specified Employees (regular arm's-length staff) and Specified Employees. Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, a "specified employee" is defined as an employee of the taxpayer who either does not deal at arm's length with the taxpayer (such as a spouse, child, or sibling of a controlling shareholder) or is a "specified shareholder" who owns, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the corporation or of any corporation related to the corporation.

5.2 Overhead Allocation: The 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Versus the Traditional Method

Pursuant to subsection 37(8) of the ITA, a claimant must elect on Form T661 for each taxation year whether to calculate its SR&ED overhead and other expenditures using the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)) or the Traditional Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)). This election governs all SR&ED projects claimed by the taxpayer in that taxation year and is legally irrevocable once Form T661 is filed for the year.

Under the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method, which is elected by over 90% of Canadian SR&ED claimants due to its administrative simplicity and financial yield, the taxpayer does not track or substantiate individual overhead invoices. Instead, under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, the taxpayer calculates a notional overhead amount equal to 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada. In Part 5 of Form T661, the taxpayer enters the eligible salary base on Line 818 (comprising directly engaged T4 salaries and wages less taxable benefits, bonuses to specified employees, employer payroll taxes, and specified employee cap reductions), multiplies that figure by 55% on Line 820 (subject to the overall PPA cap in Regulation 2900(5)), and transfers the resulting PPA to Line 502 in Part 4 of Form T661. Crucially, the PPA is never added to the subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool—because the taxpayer's actual facility rent, utilities, office supplies, and administrative salaries are already deducted in full as ordinary business expenses under section 9 of the ITA—but the PPA is added directly to "qualified expenditures" under subsection 127(9) to earn the 35% or 15% SR&ED Investment Tax Credit. Because the 55% PPA applies exclusively to T4 employee salaries and never to subcontractor invoices, engaging an in-house T4 employee rather than an independent contractor generates a substantially higher effective SR&ED credit rate.

Under the Traditional Method, no 55% proxy amount is claimed; instead, the taxpayer must identify, track, and substantiate actual overhead and other expenditures that are directly attributable (under Regulation 2900(2)) and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada in accordance with the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy. While the Traditional Method requires rigorous cost-accounting ledgers and defensible allocation keys tracing every dollar of shop-floor utilities, non-directly engaged support labour, and laboratory maintenance directly to SR&ED projects, it is advantageous for capital- and utility-intensive industrial, mining, or high-performance computing enterprises whose direct T4 R&D payroll is small relative to their direct facility or computational overhead.
5.3 Materials Consumed or Transformed, Cloud Computing Infrastructure, and Software Licences

Under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) of the ITA and paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the Income Tax Regulations, the cost of materials qualifies as an eligible SR&ED expenditure under both the Proxy and Traditional methods only if the materials are consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Materials consumed encompass physical substances or supplies—such as chemical reagents, industrial gases, destructive test specimens, or semiconductor wafers—that are destroyed or rendered virtually valueless during the experimental process. Materials transformed encompass physical raw materials, sub-assemblies, or electronic components that are integrated into an experimental prototype, pilot plant, or custom test rig during the systematic investigation. Because CRA policy defines materials strictly as tangible physical matter forming part of the body of the experimental output, general laboratory supplies (such as glassware, hand tools, or protective equipment) do not qualify as materials under the Proxy Method, though they may be claimed as directly attributable overhead under the Traditional Method.

A critical audit trap for Software-as-a-Service (SaaS), artificial intelligence, product design, and data analytics companies involves the treatment of cloud computing infrastructure (such as AWS, Google Cloud Platform, and Microsoft Azure) and software subscription licences. Under the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method, the categories of qualified current expenditures are strictly closed, and because cloud computing instances, API token fees, cloud simulation subscriptions, and CAD/SaaS software licences are intangible services rather than tangible physical matter, they do not qualify as "materials consumed or transformed" under traditional CRA administrative policy. Consequently, a taxpayer electing the 55% Proxy Method cannot claim standard cloud hosting or SaaS/CAD software subscriptions as separate current expenditures; those costs are legally deemed to be encompassed within the 55% proxy overhead allowance.

By contrast, if a data analytics or AI company elects the Traditional Method, cloud computing costs and dedicated software expenses that are directly attributable and incremental to running SR&ED experiments qualify as eligible overhead expenditures under Regulation 2900(2)(c). To substantiate cloud infrastructure costs under the Traditional Method (or under any capital/lease rules), the claimant must maintain strict accounting separation between production cloud infrastructure (live customer hosting, which belongs in Cost of Goods Sold / COGS), routine staging or quality-assurance environments, and dedicated R&D/experimental development environments. Best practice requires exporting monthly AWS, GCP, or Azure cost reports configured with granular resource tags that map specific compute clusters and model-training runs directly to eligible SR&ED project codes. Furthermore, under the legislative reforms effective after December 15, 2024, computers and software bought outright (perpetual software licences and on-premise server or GPU hardware classified as depreciable capital property) that are used all or substantially all (90% or more) for SR&ED in Canada once again qualify as eligible SR&ED capital expenditures even when the claimant elects the 55% Proxy Method.
5.4 Subcontractors, Non-Arm's-Length Transfers, and Third-Party Payments

When a taxpayer engages external contractors or research institutions to perform SR&ED work in Canada, the statutory inclusion rate depends on whether the parties deal at arm's length and the legal status of the performer. Where a claimant pays an arm's-length Canadian subcontractor (whether an incorporated vendor or an independent consultant resident and performing the work in Canada) for SR&ED performed directly "on behalf of" the claimant, 100% of the contract payment is deductible in the subsection 37(1) expenditure pool, but under subsection 127(9) of the ITA only 80% of the arm's-length contract payment enters the "qualified expenditure" base for calculating the 35% or 15% SR&ED ITC. This statutory 20% reduction strips out the subcontractor's presumed commercial profit margin and overhead so that the tax credit is awarded solely on the underlying R&D cost. To survive a CRA financial audit, the claimant must retain a written contract or statement of work (SOW) and itemized invoices explicitly identifying the eligible SR&ED activities performed in Canada on the claimant's behalf. Conversely, payments made to foreign contractors for work physically performed outside Canada are 0% eligible for both the subsection 37(1) pool and the SR&ED ITC.

Where SR&ED work is subcontracted to a non-arm's-length party (such as a parent, subsidiary, or sister corporation), the contract payment itself does not qualify for an ITC in the hands of the payer. Instead, the performing corporation incurs the underlying SR&ED expenditures, and under subsection 127(13) of the ITA the two related corporations may execute a joint election on Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) to transfer the performer's actual underlying qualified expenditures (capped at the contract amount) to the payer. Related parties must also use Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) when allocating government assistance across non-arm's-length entities.

Finally, where a taxpayer makes a third-party payment under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(ii) or (iii) of the ITA to an approved Canadian university, college, research institute, or qualifying non-profit R&D organization to carry out SR&ED in Canada related to a business class of the taxpayer—and the taxpayer is entitled to exploit the results of that research—the payment is subject to the same 80% federal ITC inclusion rate as arm's-length contracts and must be reported on Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for SR&ED) rather than in Part 2 of Form T661.
5.5 Reinstated Capital Expenditures and Shared-Use Equipment Rules

From January 1, 2014, through December 15, 2024, capital expenditures for the acquisition of depreciable property and equipment lease costs were completely excluded from SR&ED deductions and ITCs following the repeal of former paragraph 37(1)(b) enacted in Budget 2012. Effective for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024, and available for use after that date, as well as qualifying equipment lease costs first becoming payable after December 15, 2024, where applicable under the restored pre-2014 capital and lease framework), capital expenditures have been formally reinstated into the SR&ED program across two distinct statutory categories.

First, under the All or Substantially All (ASA, ≥90%) SR&ED Capital Property rules, new depreciable property—including laboratory testing apparatus, prototyping machinery, specialized tools, moulds, sensors, and dedicated R&D compute servers, but strictly excluding land, buildings, leasehold interests in buildings, and used equipment—qualifies for 100% inclusion in the section 37 expenditure pool and 100% inclusion in qualified expenditures for the SR&ED ITC if the taxpayer intends at the time of acquisition either to use the property all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life in the performance of SR&ED in Canada, or to consume all or substantially all (90% or more) of the property's value in the performance of SR&ED in Canada. For a qualifying CCPC or ECPC within its $6.0 million expenditure limit, the 35% ITC earned on ASA capital property is 40% refundable in cash under section 127.1 (generating an immediate 14% cash refund equal to 35% × 40%, plus a 21% non-refundable ITC carryforward), compared to 100% cash refundability on current expenditures.

Second, under the reinstated Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) regime, where newly acquired depreciable machinery or equipment is not used 90% or more for SR&ED, but is used primarily (more than 50%) of its operating time for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada during its first 12 months and first 24 months of operation (excluding commercial production time), up to 50% of the capital cost qualifies for the SR&ED ITC, claimed in two equal instalments of 25% in the first period (after 12 months of eligible use) and 25% in the second period (after 24 months of eligible use).
5.6 Government Assistance Stacking (NRC IRAP) and Comprehensive Worked Financial Model

Under subsection 127(18) of the ITA, a taxpayer's qualified SR&ED expenditures must be reduced by the amount of any "government assistance" or "non-government assistance" (as defined in subsection 127(9)) that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive in respect of the SR&ED at the time of filing its income tax return for the year. However, a crucial statutory feature of Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations creates one of the most lucrative non-dilutive capital-stacking mechanisms available to Canadian innovators: stacking a National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) grant with the SR&ED Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) overhead election.

When a qualifying CCPC receives a non-repayable NRC IRAP contribution that reimburses a percentage of directly engaged internal R&D salaries, subsection 127(18) requires the IRAP grant to be deducted from total SR&ED expenditures on Line 513 in Part 4 of Form T661 so that the taxpayer does not claim both an IRAP grant and an SR&ED tax credit on the same dollar of direct salary. Crucially, however, under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) overhead in Part 5 of Form T661 is calculated on the gross, unreduced eligible SR&ED salary base (Line 818) before subtracting the NRC IRAP salary grant. As a result, even if NRC IRAP reimburses 50% to 80% of an engineer's salary, the company still earns the full 55% SR&ED proxy overhead on 100% of that engineer's SR&ED salary, and then collects the 35% federal (and applicable provincial) SR&ED tax credit on both the unassisted portion of direct salary and the entire 55% proxy overhead.

6. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

In addition to the federal SR&ED tax incentive, nine Canadian provinces and one territory provide statutory provincial or territorial R&D tax credits that stack alongside the federal credit. Because provincial and territorial R&D tax credits constitute "government assistance" under subsections 127(9) and 127(18) of the federal Income Tax Act, every dollar of provincial R&D tax credit earned in a taxation year reduces the federal "qualified expenditure" pool on Line 513 of Form T661. When combined with provincial SR&ED tax credits, total combined federal-provincial credit rates can exceed 60% of eligible R&D expenditures in provinces such as Quebec. With the sole exceptions of Quebec (administered independently by Revenu Québec) and Alberta (administered independently by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration), all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits are administered directly by the Canada Revenue Agency through supplemental schedules filed with the T2 Corporation Income Tax Return (or T1 return where applicable) and adopt the federal definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) of the ITA.
6.1 Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC Tri-Tier Architecture

Ontario administers a three-tier corporate R&D tax credit structure under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) that allows qualifying corporations with a permanent establishment in Ontario to combine refundable and non-refundable credits on the same underlying Ontario SR&ED expenditures.

The primary SME incentive is the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), claimed on Schedule T2SCH566 (and integrated with Schedule T2SCH31), which provides an 8% fully refundable tax credit on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures up to an annual expenditure limit of $3.0 million (generating a maximum annual refundable cash credit of $240,000). Notably, following the 2024–2026 federal SR&ED expansion, Ontario has remained a statutory "holdout" province on the OITC, maintaining its historical $3.0 million expenditure limit (which must be shared among associated corporations) and its stricter two-factor phase-out thresholds. Specifically, a corporation's $3.0 million OITC expenditure limit begins to phase out when the associated group's prior-year federal taxable income exceeds $500,000 and is completely eliminated at $800,000, or when prior-year Ontario specified capital reaches $25 million and is completely eliminated at $50 million.

Complementing the OITC is the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), claimed on Schedule T2SCH508, which provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit (4.5% for taxation years ending before June 1, 2016) available to all corporations—regardless of whether they are CCPCs, public corporations, or foreign-controlled subsidiaries, and with no expenditure cap or capital phase-out—on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures. Crucially, a CCPC that claims the 8% refundable OITC (or 20% OBRITC) may simultaneously claim the 3.5% ORDTC on its Ontario qualified expenditures net of the OITC/OBRITC government assistance reduction, with unused ORDTC credits available for a 3-year carryback and 20-year carryforward against Ontario corporate income tax (and accompanied where applicable by Ontario Transitional Tax Debits and Credits Schedules T2SCH506 and T2SCH507).

Finally, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC), claimed on Schedule T2SCH568 along with a separate contract information Schedule T2SCH569 for each qualifying contract, provides a 20% fully refundable tax credit to any corporation carrying on business in Ontario for qualified expenditures incurred under an eligible R&D contract with an eligible Ontario research institute (such as an Ontario university, college of applied arts and technology, or hospital research institute), up to an annual qualified expenditure cap of $20 million (yielding up to $4.0 million in refundable cash credits annually).
6.2 Quebec: Transition from Legacy R&D Credits to the Unified CRIC Regime

Quebec operates an autonomous corporate and personal tax administration overseen by Revenu Québec under the Taxation Act (Quebec), supported by specialized qualification certificates issued by the Minister of Economy, Innovation and Energy (ministère de l'Économie, de l'Innovation et de l'Énergie — MEIE). Historically, Quebec's R&D tax credit system focused on Quebec R&D salaries and subcontracted research payments rather than materials or a 55% proxy overhead, while requiring claimants to surpass a statutory exclusion threshold (seuil d'exclusion ranging from $50,000 to $225,000 based on corporate asset size).

Crucially, Quebec enacted a sweeping structural reform of its innovation tax credits effective for taxation years and fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, establishing a strict statutory transition between the Legacy Regime and the New Unified CRIC Regime.

For taxation years or partnership fiscal periods beginning before March 26, 2025, claimants remain governed by the Legacy Quebec R&D Tax Credit Regime detailed in Revenu Québec guide IN-109-V (Tax Assistance for Scientific Research and Experimental Development) and mandatory deduction schedule Form RD-222-V (Deduction Respecting Scientific Research and Experimental Development Expenditures). This legacy architecture comprises four distinct refundable tax credits available to corporations, unincorporated individuals, and partnership members (excluding specified partnership members, Crown corporations, and trusts with tax-exempt or Crown beneficiaries):

items: The Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D), claimed on Form RD-1029.7-V, which provides a 14% basic refundable rate for large enterprises and an enhanced up to 30% refundable rate for qualifying SMEs (with global consolidated assets below $50 million, phasing down to 14% at $75 million) on the first $3.0 million of eligible Quebec R&D salaries and 50% of arm's-length Quebec subcontractor payments exceeding the exclusion threshold;

The Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium, claimed on Form RD-1029.8.6-V, which provides a 14% to 30% refundable credit on 80% of eligible R&D contract payments made to an eligible Quebec university entity, public research centre, or research consortium;

The Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research, claimed on Form RD-1029.8.16.1-V and requiring a qualification certificate issued by the Minister of Economy, Innovation and Energy, which provides a 14% to 30% refundable credit for arm's-length private partnership R&D projects carried out in Quebec; and

The Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium, claimed on Form RD-1029.8.9.03-V, which provides a refundable credit on eligible research consortium membership fees and dues (subject to a transitional carryover rule allowing the balance of cumulative fees or dues paid at the end of a taxation year ending after March 25, 2025, to be claimed for a taxation year ending no later than December 31, 2029).

body.text: For taxation years and fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, the four legacy credits are replaced by the unified Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization (Crédit d'impôt pour la R-D et la précommercialisation — CRIC), which may only be claimed by corporations and corporations that are members of a partnership. Under the new CRIC regime, all eligible corporations—regardless of consolidated asset size—earn a 30% fully refundable tax credit on the first $1.0 million of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures exceeding the exclusion threshold, and a 20% fully refundable tax credit on all eligible expenditures exceeding that $1.0 million tier. Furthermore, the CRIC expands Quebec's eligible expenditure base beyond traditional SR&ED to include downstream pre-commercialization activities (such as regulatory homologation, certification testing, and industrial product design) as well as capital expenditures acquired for R&D and pre-commercialization in Quebec.
6.3 Western Canada: British Columbia Express Alignment, Alberta IEG, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba
Across Western Canada, the four provinces apply distinct statutory mechanisms to incentivize business R&D and have diverged in their legislative responses to the 2024–2026 federal SR&ED reforms.

British Columbia offers a 10% SR&ED tax credit claimed on Form T666 (British Columbia Scientific Research and Experimental Development Tax Credit). Notably, British Columbia enacted express legislative alignment with the 2024–2026 federal SR&ED modernization package. Under this alignment, British Columbia extended its 10% refundable tax credit not only to qualifying CCPCs but also to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), adopted the expanded $15 million to $75 million prior-year taxable capital phase-out range, and restored capital expenditures as qualifying British Columbia SR&ED expenditures. For corporations that do not qualify for the refundable stream or for expenditures exceeding the corporation's expenditure limit, the 10% BC credit is non-refundable and may be carried back 3 years and forward 10 years.

Alberta administers its own standalone program through Alberta Treasury Board and Finance (Tax and Revenue Administration): the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG), claimed on AT1 Schedule 29 (Alberta Innovation Employment Grant) accompanied by Form AT4970 (Listing of Innovation Employment Grant Projects Claimed in Alberta). The IEG is a 100% refundable two-tier incremental grant available to qualified corporations carrying out eligible R&D in Alberta on up to $4.0 million of annual eligible expenditures. It provides an 8% base payment on eligible Alberta R&D expenditures up to the corporation's base spending level (defined as the corporation's average eligible Alberta R&D spending over the two immediately preceding taxation years) and an enhanced 20% payment (the 8% base plus a 12% incremental benefit) on eligible Alberta R&D expenditures exceeding that two-year historical base level. Consequently, a newly established Alberta R&D corporation with a $0 two-year historical base earns the full 20% refundable grant on its entire Alberta R&D spend up to $4.0 million (up to $800,000 in cash), with eligibility phasing out between $10 million and $50 million of prior-year taxable capital.

Saskatchewan provides the Saskatchewan Research and Development Tax Credit, claimed on Schedule T2SCH403, which awards CCPCs a 10% fully refundable tax credit up to an annual limit of $1.0 million in qualifying Saskatchewan SR&ED expenditures (maximum $100,000 cash refund), and a 10% non-refundable tax credit on qualifying expenditures by CCPCs exceeding $1.0 million as well as on all qualifying expenditures by non-CCPCs.

Manitoba provides the Manitoba Research and Development Tax Credit, claimed on Schedule T2SCH380, which awards a 15% tax credit on eligible Manitoba SR&ED expenditures with no annual expenditure limit. For in-house R&D conducted by the corporation in Manitoba, half of the credit (7.5%) is immediately refundable and the other half (7.5%) is non-refundable; however, for eligible R&D carried out in Manitoba under contract with a qualifying post-secondary or research institute, the entire 15% credit is 100% refundable.
6.4 Atlantic Canada, Northern Territories, and Complete Provincial/Territorial Matrix

All three participating Atlantic provinces—New Brunswick (Schedule T2SCH360), Newfoundland and Labrador (Schedule T2SCH301 for corporations and Form T1129 for individuals), and Nova Scotia (Schedule T2SCH340)—along with the Yukon territory offer a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit on eligible provincial or territorial SR&ED expenditures, with no annual expenditure cap and no taxable capital phase-out, plus an additional 5% refundable credit (20% total) in the Yukon for eligible amounts paid or payable to Yukon University. Conversely, Prince Edward Island (PEI), the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut do not offer a territorial or provincial R&D income tax credit, meaning that claimants in those three jurisdictions claim the federal 35% or 15% SR&ED ITC on 100% of their qualified expenditure pool without any provincial assistance reduction.

body.text: 7. Compliance Governance, Prescribed Filing Procedures, and Audit Defence
7.1 Prescribed Forms, Part 2 Technical Narratives, and Claim Preparer Penalties

To submit a legally valid SR&ED claim under the Income Tax Act, a taxpayer must file an income tax return accompanied by Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim, guided by CRA Publication T4088, Guide to Form T661) and either Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) for corporate claimants or Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credits (Individuals)) for unincorporated individuals and trusts, along with any applicable supplemental forms (Form T1145, Form T1146, Form T1174, and Form T1263). Electronic transmission using CRA-certified commercial tax preparation software is mandatory for almost all Canadian corporations, whereas individuals, trusts, and partnerships filing paper returns mail their claim package to their designated CRA Tax Centre.

In Part 2 of Form T661 (Project Information), the claimant must submit a project-by-project technical narrative establishing how the claimed work satisfies the statutory requirements of subsection 248(1). Where a claimant undertakes more than 20 SR&ED projects in a taxation year, the CRA permits the claimant at the time of initial filing to submit Part 2 descriptions for only the 20 largest projects in dollar value, though the CRA reserves the legal authority to request Part 2 submissions for some or all of the remaining projects during review, and failure to provide them results in mandatory disallowance of the expenditures for those projects. Additionally, if a federal agency has designated a project as "classified information" for national security reasons, the claimant must complete Section B of Part 2 on a separate physical sheet retained on-site for inspection and submit a formal notification letter with Form T661 rather than transmitting classified details over public channels.

Section B of Part 2 enforces strict maximum word limits across three sequential technical prompts that correspond directly to the CRA's eligibility guidelines and the Northwest Hydraulic judicial framework. On Line 242 (What scientific or technological uncertainties did you attempt to overcome? — maximum 350 words), the technical author must establish the baseline of publicly available scientific or technological knowledge and explain the specific system-level limitation, conflict, or constraint that could not be resolved through standard engineering practice. On Line 244 (What work did you perform in the tax year to overcome the technological obstacles/uncertainties described in Line 242? — maximum 700 words), the author must chronologically describe the specific hypotheses formulated to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty, the systematic experiments or analyses conducted during the taxation year to test those hypotheses, the quantitative and qualitative results observed, and the logical conclusions drawn. On Line 246 (What scientific or technological advancements did you achieve as a result of the work described in Line 244? — maximum 350 words), the author must articulate the new scientific or technological knowledge or capability generated as a result of the investigation. In Section C of Part 2, the claimant inventories the contemporaneous supporting evidence generated as the work progressed—such as project planning records, source code repositories and commit logs (GitHub), issue-tracking tickets (Jira), engineering notebooks, test logs, photographs provided by the claimant, and physical prototypes.

Under Part 9 of Form T661, every claimant must provide complete claim preparer disclosures indicating whether an external consultant, accounting firm, or automated platform prepared or assisted in preparing the claim. Where a third-party claim preparer assisted (noting that traditional SR&ED consultants typically charge contingency fees ranging from 15% to 25% of the refund amount), Part 9 mandates disclosure of the preparer's identification, billing arrangement code, and total fee; if no claim preparer was used, the claimant must still complete Lines 935, 970, and 975 certifying internal preparation. Pursuant to subsections 162(5.1) through (5.3) of the ITA, any failure to provide complete and accurate claim preparer information in Part 9 triggers a $1,000 statutory penalty for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally liable, and under Regulation 2902 claim preparation fees are prescribed expenditures that must be excluded from qualified SR&ED expenditures.
7.2 The Strict 18-Month Statutory Reporting Bar Under Subsection 220(2.2)

The most unforgiving procedural deadline in Canadian R&D tax law is the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline governed by subsection 37(11), paragraph 127(9)(m), and subsection 220(2.2) of the Income Tax Act. Under paragraph 150(1)(a) of the ITA, a corporation's T2 income tax return filing due date is six months after the end of its taxation year. Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m), a taxpayer's SR&ED reporting deadline is 12 months after its income tax return filing due date for the year—establishing an absolute statutory deadline of 18 months after the end of the taxation year for corporations (for example, a corporation with a December 31, 2025 fiscal year-end faces a T2 filing due date of June 30, 2026, and a final SR&ED reporting deadline of June 30, 2027).

While a corporation may file its standard T2 return on time at the six-month mark and subsequently file an amended return adding Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 at any time on or before the 18-month reporting deadline, subsection 220(2.2) of the ITA explicitly strips the Minister of National Revenue of any discretionary authority to extend the 18-month SR&ED deadline. A claim cannot be filed or amended to add new expenditures or projects after the 18-month deadline has expired; missing the 18-month date by even a single day permanently and irrevocably bars the SR&ED deduction and investment tax credit for that taxation year.
7.3 Bifurcated CRA Review Architecture, Advisory Services, and Dispute Resolution

Upon filing, an SR&ED claim is evaluated by the CRA's risk-assessment system, which was modernized in 2025 to deploy AI-supported claim screening that accelerates low-risk filings while selecting complex or higher-risk claims for examination. For refundable claims that are Accepted As Filed (AAF) without audit, the CRA's service standard is 60 calendar days from receipt of a complete claim; for claims selected for technical and financial review, the service standard is 180 calendar days. To assist businesses before an audit occurs, the CRA operates the First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS)—a free half-day educational consultation where CRA specialists advise first-time claimants on eligibility, allowable expenditures, and contemporaneous documentation—as well as the Optional Pre-Claim Approval / Pre-Claim Review program, under which a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) conducts a mandatory or requested meeting and issues a written technical eligibility decision within 8 weeks of receiving a completed pre-claim application, alongside ongoing Account Executive (AE) and SR&ED Service Visit programs.

When a filed claim is selected for audit, the examination is conducted under the CRA Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors by two distinct specialists: a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA), who evaluates whether the claimed projects satisfy the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) of the ITA, and a Financial Reviewer (FR), who determines whether the claimed expenditures comply with section 37, section 127, and Regulation 2900 based on the RTA's technical determinations. During site visits, RTAs interview technical leads, examine physical prototypes and contemporaneous records (noting that CRA security rules strictly prohibit RTAs from taking photographs at a claimant's premises, requiring reliance on claimant-supplied photographs and documents), and compile an official SR&ED Review Report co-signed by the RTA and approved by the Research and Technology Manager (RTM). In Section 2 of the SR&ED Review Report, each claimed project receives one of five formal administrative determinations: AW (All Work) where all reviewed work meets the definition of SR&ED; SW (Some Work) where only a portion of the reviewed work qualifies; NW (No Work) where no claimed work qualifies; UN (Unsubstantiated) where the claimant's records are inadequate under the ITA to determine eligibility; or AAF (Accepted As Filed) where the project is accepted without technical determination.

If an RTA or FR issues an adverse draft report, the claimant can pursue a structured four-stage escalation and dispute resolution pathway. In the first stage, the claimant submits a comprehensive written technical and financial rebuttal supported by primary contemporaneous evidence directly to the RTA and FR before the review report is signed. In the second stage, if working-level disagreements remain unresolved, the claimant escalates the dispute to the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) and Financial Review Manager, and may file Form RC532 (Request for Administrative Second Review of an SR&ED Claim) to request a formal administrative review of procedural compliance. In the third stage, once a formal Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued, the claimant files a formal Notice of Objection within 90 calendar days to trigger an independent administrative review by the CRA Appeals Branch. Finally, in the fourth stage, if the CRA Appeals Branch confirms the disallowance, the claimant may appeal to the Tax Court of Canada—where the appeal is adjudicated de novo under the five-question test in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen—with a further right of appeal on questions of law to the Federal Court of Appeal.
